articles.title: THE BLESSEDNESS OF THE CONTROL OF CHRIST
articles.author: C. Middleton

paragraphs.text: What I have before me is quite a simple thought, but I believe the simple things in the divine realm are well worth going over. The apostle Paul in writing to the Philippians says he is writing the same things and comments. For you it is safe (Philippians 3: 1). It is safe for us to go over some of the simple things of christianity, for we know in recent times of a great many who have turned aside, and generally we find that when persons turn aside it is because they have not really learnt their first lessons.

So I am thinking of these persons who were brought under the control of Christ—and in reality that is what we accept for ourselves when we own Jesus as Lord. If we stay in that position we are safe. Nobody goes astray who is under the control of Christ. That is how we begin, and, if only we continue like that, we are preserved.

In this scripture we have, first of all, this great light; that means the coming in of Jesus. We do not get here the expansion of all that this great light means, but the very fact of the Lord being here on earth, His incarnation, His growing up here, meant that the great light of christianity, which is developed right through the New Testament, was there. Persons did not, in fact, realise how great the light was, yet it says, “The people sitting

in darkness has seen a great light, and to those sitting in the country and shadow of death, to them has light sprung up”. This is God’s intervention, Christ coming in. There they were sitting in darkness, but, when the light came in, they were not intended to go on sitting; they were intended to move. That is a principle in Scripture all the way through, that when light comes in it is intended to make a difference to people, to make them move. I suppose there were those who continued sitting—and they were all the more responsible because of having been in the presence of the light. But normally the effect of the light is to produce movement. That applies today. We would not say that any true believer is in the fullest sense of the word sitting in darkness, but he may be to some extent in the dark. He may say, ‘I am sitting quietly at home’; but the light is intended to make him move. The light has come in in order to take control of him, not simply so that he can enjoy the shining in a distant kind of way.

Now the Lord coming in was the great light, and that was intended to affect everybody. We know that some refused it—there were some who loved darkness rather than light. I believe we are all here because we love the light, we love the Lord. We can never exhaust the knowledge of the Lord, the greatness of the light. Paul got an impression of that on the day he was converted. He could not see for the glory of that light, and within a short time he was preaching that Jesus is the Son of God. He had got that appreciation of Christ. Much later on, in Philippians, we find he is still pursuing, “On account of the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord”, Philippians 3: 8. He knew the Lord far better than any of us, I suppose, nevertheless, he still wanted to go on to know more.

This thought of a great light is a very wonderful thing, yet what the Lord says when He begins His preaching is very simple. He does not go over the whole realm of what is connected with the revelation; He just speaks of repenting, “for the kingdom of the heavens has drawn nigh”. The very reference to the heavens gives us a sense of greatness. As the heavens are higher than the earth, we are told, so are God’s thoughts higher than our thoughts (Isaiah 55: 9). What an immense difference between them! The greatest thoughts we have are eclipsed by what comes from heaven. On the part of the people repentance was needed. It was not without cause that they were sitting in darkness; they were not without their own responsibility. That is why they were there. They might say that a great deal had contributed to it, due to the power of the enemy; but repentance was called for. Repentance is a deepening work that can very well go on with all of us. When the Ephesians had left their first love the only way back was to repent (Revelation 2: 5). That means a real revolution in a man’s soul.

Well, this was wonderful news for these people. Instead of darkness and a hopeless condition of things, “the kingdom of the heavens has drawn nigh”. That means that a tremendous power has come in from heaven. In a certain sense the kingdom of the heavens was established when Christ went back into heaven and now, thank God, there are those on earth who are governed by the light from heaven. Our lives are to be controlled by the One who is in heaven; that is what the kingdom of the heavens means. Heaven is now to have control. It is not a control that is in force everywhere on the earth. It is a most extraordinary thing how God, for the time being, tolerates the will of man, which resists His will on earth.
Yet, in the midst of all the lawlessness that there is, we can, thank God, have our part amongst those who are controlled from heaven, and by the One who is in heaven.

When we come to the next paragraph it becomes a more personal matter. Here the Lord is walking and He finds these two brothers and calls them. He says, “Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men”. This brings in the direct personal link of the Lord with the individual. Each is to come after Him, and then He speaks of what He will make them. Of course this was very special in the case of Peter particularly, and of Andrew also. The Lord had great thoughts for them. They were amongst the twelve, who were to bear the brunt of things and carry on the testimony in a hostile scene when the Lord had gone. They had a comparatively short time of training. I suppose by the time they had that heavy responsibility on their shoulders they had known the Lord only three or four years. I expect the great majority of us here have known the Lord longer than that. What a tremendous responsibility these men were capable of sustaining! The Lord had made something of them. I suppose, if we are in His hands, it would be right to apply this in some degree to any one of us. The Lord does not mean many of us to have a very outstanding place, no doubt, but He can make something of us—that is, if we are in His hands. I suppose there are some who are so inclined to go their own way that the Lord cannot make much of them, and perhaps many of us have given Him a lot of trouble. Yet I believe the Lord would make something of us. In a day of small things how valuable every brother and sister is! But they are only valuable as they are what the Lord intends to make them. It is not human ordination, as we get all around us, it is what
the Lord is making of people.

Then you see what a response there was. These men move immediately. It is remarkable the effect the Lord’s call had upon them. We might wonder why they did not want a week or two to think it over, but divine speaking is intended to produce an immediate result. That is what we should normally look for, and it should be so with us. We know God speaks once, yea twice, and I suppose with many of us He may have spoken a good many times before we moved. But Peter and Andrew are a good example, they moved at once. So did James and John—they had the same call from the Lord, though not in quite the same words—He does not say what He is going to make them. Yet we know He did make use of them. What a valuable man John was particularly, and no doubt James too, though we do not know so much about him. The Lord took a special interest in these persons, but it is not meant only for them. They are a sample of what the Lord calls us for. He would have us to realise that that call gives a personal link between Him and ourselves. It is not only that the glad tidings is available to everyone, and that He is Lord of all, but there is a special link between Him and the one He calls. We want to have a sense of that, that the Lord Jesus has not called us for nothing; He has not called us without any intention as to what He is going to do with us. He has called us having in view that He wants us.

The immediate point is that He called them and they went after Him. They, “having left the ship and their father, immediately followed him”. It is stressed in their case that they had to leave their father. In the case of Peter and Andrew it is more what the Lord had in view for them. Both points are important. The Lord had to take

precedence over their father. This does not alter the fact that a man is to honour his father and mother; in fact the Lord had to speak very seriously about the kind of thing that we come across today, that persons are not permitted to do any more for father or mother on the plea that they are so devoted to the Lord. The Lord condemns that; He says, “And ye no longer suffer him to do anything for his father or his mother”, Mark 7: 12. No doubt James and John would have done something for Zebedee if he needed it, no doubt they would honour their father; but when it is a question of priorities the Lord takes first place above father or mother, wife or children. “Come after me”, just simply means that. So they followed Him.

We are going over things we know well, and one can only say that it is safe to go over them. They are very simple, yet they are very blessed. The Lord is to have control. The fact that we have only a mere fraction of the brethren here today who belong to the Lord in this place is evidence that there are a great many with whom He has not got control. But then we cannot just assume because of a right position that the Lord has got control of us. Thank God if He has in any degree. But with these men it was complete and immediate and they went after Him.

Then they see what a wonderful system they are brought into. They are linked up with the One who goes round the whole of Galilee, teaching and preaching and healing. He was “preaching the glad tidings of the kingdom”. This is wonderful good news for men, that the kingdom has come. We may think of kingdom truth as being very simple and basic. Well, it is; but it is very good. It is glad tidings. We might challenge ourselves whether we are enjoying it as much as we should. The

queen of Sheba came a long way to see what the kingdom of Solomon was like, and to get to know him, and she found it was twice as good as she had heard, or more than that. What a wonderful place it was! It was a safe place—there was no evil occurrent, and it was a wealthy place. The kingdom is a place where persons are subdued. With David you get more the power to subdue, and with Solomon the wealth and display and the wisdom, all that is to be found in the kingdom. So the glad tidings of the kingdom meant that however much God had borne in patience with conditions up to this moment, the kingdom had now come in and the evil had to give way. We wait for the Lord’s coming before evil finally has to give way everywhere, but in the souls of those who are affected by the light of the kingdom the power of the enemy is broken now as the Lord has control. Now that is what we have to see to, that He really does have control. The Lord’s coming in brings most wonderful blessing. When He gets a place in a man’s heart it brings blessing to that man. When He came into the house of Zacchaeus He brought salvation to the house. And in a meeting, when the Lord gets His place there is blessing in the meeting. We expect that and experience it, yet it is possible to have meetings where blessing is not really enjoyed very much, and you can trace that to the Lord not really having control; there is somebody there over whom He has not got control. Once He has control everything prospers.

Then the Lord is not only teaching and preaching but He is healing. This is a remarkably comprehensive list of those who were healed. It is seen that the Lord can deal with everything. We do not see Him doing a great deal today in healing people’s bodies, but I believe what is suggested here is that there is no disease in the soul of

anyone which cannot be healed by the Lord. If all the people with all their troubles in this locality or any other locality were to come to the Lord today, they would find that He has just as much power as He had in this record here. He could deal with them all. Whatever troubles we have in our souls He can deal with them all. We were speaking of the man who calls himself a “wretched man” in Romans 7; he realised that deliverance was found in having to do with Christ. It was not so much that he learned the doctrine better, but he says, “I thank God, through Jesus Christ our Lord”, Romans 7: 25. He realises that it is Christ who is the Deliverer. And, of course, a person does get delivered when he gets to know Christ. He becomes his Object instead of himself, and that has a wonderful delivering effect. So this great crowd, every one of them, got the gain of having to do with the Lord, “He healed them”. This healing is always an individual matter. The Lord may give us blessing all together, and everybody enjoys it, but when it comes to healing it is the Lord’s own touch to the individual. You have to do with Him, both in regard to the initial call and in regard to your exercises where healing may be needed.

Now in the next chapter He goes up into the mountain and sits down. And then we find the crowds to some extent get left behind and the disciples come to Him. That shows that He had control of them. He did not order them up into the mountain, but the disciples realised it was well worth going up into that mountain in order to get to the Lord. Peter later on gives expression to his appreciation of this when he says, in a very testing time, “Lord, to whom shall we go? thou hast words of life eternal”, John 6: 68. Others were going away, but Peter knew he must keep near the Lord—and it was well worth while keeping
near the Lord, “Thou hast words of life eternal”. Peter was not only thinking of what the Lord had communicated, but that, if he kept near Him, he could continue to get communications.

The Lord’s disciples had some sense of that, so they went up the mountain in order to get to the Lord; and then it says, “Having opened his mouth, he taught them”. Now they come into the region of the teaching. We all have to be taught. We even have to he taught of God to love one another; that is one of the things that the Thessalonians were taught, and you are taught everything in christianity. The teaching goes right on to what we get in Ephesians, and a disciple is one who is ready for it. It means that the Lord has control of us as we realise that it is well worth going up a mountain or doing anything in order to get where the Lord is and where His teaching is going on.

So He says, “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of the heavens”. I did not think of going on further than that, but I think these persons who are poor in spirit are rather like those we were speaking of earlier today, who were subdued. They are not high-spirited, uncontrollable people, but they are those the Lord has had to do with, so that the power He has to subdue all things to Himself has already affected them. It would be good if we were all like that, poor in spirit and really subdued to Christ. Then He adds, “Theirs is the kingdom of the heavens”. The whole wealth of the kingdom is open to them, and the whole power of the kingdom is available to support them. When we look round and see what power the enemy has in the world—and it seems to be on the increase, with lawlessness abounding you might wonder how the saints can get through according to God. Well, the power of the kingdom is in support of these persons of whom the Lord speaks as the poor in spirit. You have the wealth of the kingdom and the power of the kingdom for those who are really subdued. If we are really brought under the control of Christ it brings us into this avenue of the greatest blessing and thus we come into His presence where the teaching is going on and the blessing and power of the kingdom are known.

articles.title: THE HEART OF GOD AND THE HEART OF MAN
articles.author: A. A. Bellamy

paragraphs.text: I desire to speak of the heart of God and the heart of man. They are contrasted in Scripture. After the flood, it is said that “Jehovah said in his heart, I will no more henceforth curse the ground on account of Man” (Genesis 8: 21); the curse had been removed and the disposition of God’s heart was to bless, and that in spite of man’s heart—which, as that scripture says, is evil from his youth. The heart of God is disposed towards men in blessing. He “desires that all men should be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth”, 1 Timothy 2: 4.

In the first passage God speaks of a man that He had found, a man after His heart. The very nature, the very attributes, of the blessed God Himself have been declared in the Man that He has found after His heart. There would not be

anything for us, dear friends, if God first had not found such a Man. The Man I refer to is Jesus. No one like Him had ever been upon the earth before, and no one since. Divine perfection was there in a Man, in flesh and blood condition—the very condition in which we are, sin apart. The reality of the manhood of Jesus is a wonderful thing to contemplate; He was indeed the Man after God’s heart.

So we have our attention focused upon Christ as the Man after God’s heart. He raised up David, and He raised up Jesus. He raised Him up from among the dead. It is a living Saviour that we present to men. It is a wonderful thing, dear friends, that God should speak to us of this Man after His heart! God is drawing our attention to Christ, and to the fact that His delight is in Him—“This is my beloved Son, in whom I have found my delight”, Matthew 17: 5.

Who can measure what God has found in Jesus, and what Jesus has effected for God? How great is the work that He accomplished! He came to do the will of God. We have in the Old Testament through David, “Then said I, Behold, I come, in the volume of the book it is written of me—To do thy good pleasure, my God ...”, Psalm 40: 7, 8. Adam was the first man, but he has been superseded by Christ. Christ is the second Man out of heaven. There is no need for a third man. The second Man is the One who came to do the will of God, and He has done it; He has done it. “I have glorified thee on the earth, I have completed the work which thou gavest me that I should do it” (John 17: 4); there is no need for another to come. John the baptist, when in prison, doubted for a moment whether Christ was the coming One. He sent a message, “Art thou he that is coming, or are we to wait for another?”,
Luke 7: 19. We are not waiting for another; we are not waiting for a third man. The second Man has already come, and He is the Man after God’s own heart.

In Jesus we see that God’s disposition is to bless. We see that in Jesus here as He was amongst men, in all the pathway of love which He trod—down to the cross and to the grave. Oh how vast is the work that Jesus has accomplished upon the cross! Well has it been said that it is the centre-point of eternity—the cross of Christ. He died for sinners, and before He died He bore the sins in His body on the tree of all who believe on Him. Are we among that number? How serious not to be among the number of those that believe. You may come now within the ranks of those that believe, and we have a prospect before us, a glorious prospect, that the One who was once here in lowly guise will come again in glory. He is going to change society from the top to the bottom—every strata; Christ is going to change everything. “The earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of Jehovah as the waters cover the sea”, (Habakkuk 2: 14), and He is the One who will do it. How great He is!

Have you by faith a link with Him? Can you say, ‘He is mine’? Can you say, ‘He is my Saviour, my Lord’? Do you acknowledge His rights over you? They are absolute. No other has prior rights over us because He died for us. So let us seek to carry into practice the acknowledgment of His rights over us.
I turn to my second scripture. This man, Simon, was not a believer in a real sense. Although it says he believed and was baptised he was really an imposter. One is coming of whom the

Lord said, “If another come in his own name, him ye will receive” (John 5: 43)—the antichrist, the man of sin, full of deceit. He will deceive people—that kind of man; and already there have been many who have borne that character, not the antichrist, but, as John says, “many antichrists”, 1 John 2: 18. They are against Christ. They assert their own importance and greatness, as this man did. He said he was “some great one”. Whoever he was is neither here nor there, there is only one Man who is great in God’s estimation and that is Christ, and only He is to be great in our estimation.

Now this man came amongst those who believed and he noticed that power was operating, the power of the Holy Spirit, and he actually exposed himself when he offered money that he also might have that power. Peter (I do not go into all the details) discerned this man, and that his heart was not upright. What a solemn position for anyone to be in—any man or woman or young person—to have a heart that is not upright before God. What could be done for this man? He had heard the gospel; he had moved amongst those who had preached the gospel; it even says that he believed and was baptised; but he was an imposter. Peter says, “Thy heart is not upright before God. Repent ...”. Did he repent? We do not know. Scripture is solemn in what it does not tell us. Some persons come so near to the blessing, and the Spirit of God does not tell us whether they received it or not. One man said, “In a little thou persuadest me to become a Christian”, Acts 26: 28. Was he persuaded? We do not know; the Spirit of God just leaves it there—almost persuaded to be a Christian!
I pass on to my third scripture concerning two men. One goes to meet the other, and they both have right hearts. That is a fine thing! “Is thy heart right, as my heart is with thy heart? ... It

is”. That is a little picture of what we speak of as ‘fellowship’. Fellowship is the portion of persons whose hearts are right with God first, right vertically; and then right horizontally, “Is thy heart right, as my heart is with thy heart?”. It was so with these men. One gave the other his hand. We read in Galatians 2: 9 of “the right hands of fellowship”. Paul had been commissioned by the Lord to carry the glad tidings to the gentiles, and he met James and Cephas and John who were to carry the glad tidings to the circumcision. These three men, we are told, gave Paul and Barnabas “the right hands of fellowship”. O, dear friends, there is such a thing as that, here upon the earth at the present time—the fellowship of God’s Son. How dignified it is! It is also the fellowship of Christ’s death. How exclusive it is! And if it is the fellowship of Christ’s death, then nothing should be admitted within the circle of that fellowship (not even in my heart, nor in anyone’s heart) inconsistent with the death of Christ.

Well, these are searching but encouraging matters; first to see what is in God’s heart towards all men, and, so to speak, to read the heart of God in the Person of Jesus—in the work that He has done, in the service He is rendering from the highest point in the universe at this present time—and then to be warned about a heart that is not upright before God. Peter said to that man, “Repent”. He had said that earlier when he preached in Jerusalem, “Repent, and be baptised, each one of you ... for remission of sins, and ye will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit”, Acts 2: 38. Jesus is the giver of the Holy Spirit. The Samaritan woman came to that; “Sir”, she said, “give me this water, that I may not thirst nor come here to draw”, John 4: 15. She came to know Christ as the giver of the Holy Spirit.

Then these two men whose hearts were right, one with the other—not the thickness of a piece of tissue paper between those two brothers! Oh what a state of things that is, thy heart right with my heart. Dear friends, let us see these things, let us commit ourselves to them, let us go in for them. There is nothing like them in the world. There is nothing so worth while as to become a christian. May the Lord bless the word.

Along with our inquiry, dear brethren, regarding what we have and what we possess, there runs another thought and that is what we are. In this first scripture we read, “and ye are Christ’s” or “and ye Christ’s”. Many scriptures come into it, and I am sure that the brethren can fill in other scriptures as we go, but I think it is a wonderful thing for us to consider what we are, and who we are. I am not speaking now at the moment collectively, I am speaking about you and me as individuals.

Think of how the Scripture speaks, “as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God”. Another scripture is, “Do ye not know that your body is temple of the Holy Spirit?”, 1 Corinthians 6: 19. These things are all for us to consider, who we are and what we are. One scripture says that “God is not God of the dead, but of the living”, Matthew 22: 32. So there is a wonderful area of life, as Abigail said to David that he was “bound in the bundle of the living”, 1 Samuel 25: 29. I trust that we may have some impression this afternoon of this area of God’s grace and God’s mercy. It is an area where God is blessing, an area where God has great delight, and it is made up of these persons. It is not a nebulous thing, you know, the land; God’s inheritance in the saints is not a nebulous thing, it is real and concrete, and I trust we may be helped to lay hold of it. Christianity is not merely an idea. Men have had ideas over the centuries, many ideas from great thinkers. Think of the greatness of the minds of these men, the great thinkers of history—Plato, Socrates, Aristotle, and others. What thinkers they were, what men of ability, that they were able to conceive ideas and scientific things which have held even to our day. I think we must regard the ability of man’s mind. Think of the measure to which civilization at the present day has grown, and the scientific advances of men; I am more impressed about it as I think about it, and yet the apostle says, “The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God”.

Well now, what thoughts go through your mind when you come to that point where you see the greatness of the mind and development of man on the one hand, and then the Scripture says it is foolishness with God? What goes on in our minds when we get to that point? Do you reject the scriptural statement as foolishness? Are we sympathetic with God? Or do you reject it? We are forced to acknowledge the skill which men have, we cannot deny it; we cannot deny it, for example, in medicine and in space. We cannot deny it, but is it to

regulate us? Is it to rule us? Is it to influence our desires, our wishes? Is it to influence our lives, our aims, our goals? I was reading about a person who has set aside money for a ticket to go to the moon. I just use it as an illustration of what people are setting as their goal, their aim. Well, what foolishness when you think of it, over against the wisdom of God, when you think of it over against what God has given us, what He has made available to us for our taking.

Think of the “free gift”; Romans 5: 15 speaks of God’s “free gift in grace”. Think of it, dear brethren, let it sink into our hearts and dominate our lives, what God has done, what God has, and what He says we are. “And ye are Christ’s”. He has redeemed you; and then it speaks in another place of the assembly that God “has purchased with the blood of his own”, Acts 20: 28. Think of the blood of Jesus. Think of how that comes into your life and mine. “Ye Christ’s”, that is what Paul says. Are you Christ’s? One might speak to a person on the street and say, ‘Are you the Lord’s?’. That is a good question; I would just put that question to you. Are you Christ’s? Well, that is what this scripture says. Of course, Paul is speaking to believers here, persons who he knows have put their faith in Jesus. It is a wonderful thing to come under the shelter of the blood of that One, as Peter says, “Precious blood, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot”, 1 Peter 1: 19. Oh what precious blood it was!—the blood of Jesus.

The next thing—we did not read it—is, “Do ye not know that your body is temple of the Holy Spirit which is in you, which ye have of God?”, 1 Corinthians 6: 19. The apostle is asking this question. Do you know that? Then he says, “Glorify now then God in your body”. I desire to present this matter

in as attractive a way as possible, that you might be lured—and that is a right word, the scripture says, “I will allure her”, Hosea 2: 14. I would desire that we might be allured into the active life of christianity, the active enjoyment of it. So this is one of the first things, “Do ye not know that your body is temple of the Holy Spirit?”. Think of the greatness of it—over against all the wisdom of men that we have spoken about; here is a divine Person, the Holy Spirit of God, indwelling persons. Your body is a temple, you become a temple as the Spirit dwells there, so Paul just says, “Glorify now then God in your body”. That is the word in itself, and I could not enlarge upon it. Just do it!

Then we come to Romans 8, “As many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God”, the greatest thought of what you are, a son of God. Think about Moses—would he be called son of Pharaoh’s daughter? Young people often aspire to great things; have you thought of what it would have been to be called a son of the daughter of Pharaoh, that great monarch? Maybe Moses would have had a pyramid; he might have, the Pharaohs had them. Moses might have succeeded him, he might have been ruler of Egypt, he might have conquered lands. Think of what it would mean. Do you aspire to such things today? The scripture says, “As many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God”. There is nothing finer at the present day, dear brethren, than to be among the sons of God. Nothing finer, absolutely. You could be high up in business, you could have the greatest job in the world, you could be the President or Prime Minister, or whatever. But sons of God are persons led by the Spirit; that is, they are not doing their own will, they are subject to the Spirit of God. They are a temple, the Spirit of

God dwells in them, and they are led by the Spirit. How important is the leading of the Spirit of God in this present day, for it says, “There are gods many, and lords many”, 1 Corinthians 8: 5. I think we can each one assess that, as we are conscious of what is going on in the world, that there are lords many and gods many; that is, men are dominated by certain things, they will go to all lengths, they will sometimes die in the pursuit of their god, money or power—it is usually one of these two, and it eventuates in power. “Yet to us there is one God, the Father”.

Well, dear brethren, there is what men are led by, but what I would like to present, and entrance your heart with, is the thought of being sons of God, being, as it also says, “children of God”, “heirs of God, and Christ’s joint heirs”. It is a wonderful area for us to develop and I am sure that none of us has developed it to its fullest extent. The wonderful area and scope that there is for us to enter into in the appreciation of divine things, has barely been scratched. I often think of the border of Judah in the book of Joshua; it says, “as far as ... the great sea” (Joshua 15: 47), as though you get to a point where there is just vastness beyond, and that is what you find when you come to the point of realising that you are one of the sons of God, and that God has made these things true of you. Then we find that there is just a vastness beyond that has hardly been touched in the knowledge of God and in the enjoyment of divine things.

How wonderful it is, and if only we could just be affected by it more at the present time, as the apostle says in the last scripture we read, “for our commonwealth has its existence in the heavens”. Oh what a commonwealth, dear brethren, what a country we belong to! We are strangers and

sojourners here; you are here in Canada, but our commonwealth—we belong to the same commonwealth, dear brethren—“our commonwealth has its existence in the heavens”. That is, it is not made here and taken up by God, but it is made there, and it exists there, and it is ever there; that is our land.

Well, I trust that these things will just sink into our hearts. I cannot say much about them, because of not being too much in the good of them myself, and yet seeking to be moved by them. I trust that each one here acknowledges what he is, a son of God. God has set you up, as it were, in this wonderful and exalted place. I repeat, there is nothing finer than to be a son of God, even if you were the most despised person in this world. Paul says in 1 Corinthians 4: 13, “We are become as the offscouring of the world, the refuse of all, until now”. Think of Paul saying that, a man who was a Hebrew of Hebrews, educated in the finest school of his day, “at the feet of Gamaliel” (Acts 22: 3), the greatest teacher of his day, and yet he says, “We are become as the offscouring of the world”; that man was a son of God.

Oh how wonderful it is to think that whatever place you may have here does not matter, but what place you have there—and what a place it is! It is what is true of you as a son of God, and one who enjoys his commonwealth, “our commonwealth” which “has its existence in the heavens”; that is where our heart is, that is where our minds are. That is where everything is, we are centred right around that thought, the commonwealth, “sons of God”, “children of God”, “heirs of God”, and “Christ’s joint heirs”—all these things, and you think of how wonderful they are. We could go on, we could expand on what we are in a collective sense, the brethren of Christ, the bride of Christ, think of all this area. How little,

perhaps, we touch it, dear brethren; how much more there is for us to go in for. I trust that our appetites may be stimulated, as the psalm says, “Taste and see that Jehovah is good”, Psalm 34: 8. Well, I trust that each one will go in for it put your mouth into it, as it were, begin to have a desire and an appetite for God’s things, and I am sure that each one will find the enjoyment that there is in being a son of God, this wonderful privilege and place that God has given us, for His name’s sake.

‘I DO IT FOR LOVE!’ We stopped at a petrol pump outside a country shop. The lady in charge was very busy, evidently managing both shop and pump. After serving some customers in the shop, she hurried out to us. ‘You’re busy!’, we commented. Brightly she answered, ‘I do it for love—I do it for my husband’. That set us thinking about love as the greatest motive in the universe. The believer has learned divine love and, by the Spirit, it is to become formative in him. Paul says, “Let all things ye do be done in love”, 1 Corinthians 16: 14. That great love chapter, 1 Corinthians 13, shows that, apart from love, the greatest knowledge, the greatest self-sacrifice, are worth nothing. But where love is the pure spring and motive of any little service, how precious it is to heaven!

“GIVE THYSELF TO READING” Following the death of Mrs. G. Wellershaus, of Endbach, some of her copies of this magazine were returned to us and it was affecting to look over them and see the diligence with which they had been read, and the reaction in her on soul. For instance, some passages relating to communion with divine Persons had been underlined. One of them was a reference to the entry in the index to Mr. Darby’s ‘Letters’, ‘The good of being alone with God’. In another place a brother had commented in relation to 2 Peter 1: 21—‘Mr. Darby actually uses the word they “spake under the power of the Holy Spirit”, but in his note he says, ‘spake as borne by’ the Holy Spirit, almost as if the Holy Spirit was carrying them along’. In the margin our sister had quoted the line, ‘My soul is all transported’. That was her reaction to the word, the enlargement of the impression as it echoed in her soul. That surely is the way to read, our affections and minds sensitive and ready to respond to the impressions presented. There is much for divine pleasure in that.

But then, in chapter 4 (of 2 Timothy) you have the work brought out for the servant. We are not to let our hands hang down. In the difficult days, work is to go on … There is work set out for Timothy. I think we ought to bear in mind that no circumstances in this world can interfere with assembly principles. The Father does not come into view in this epistle; it is more the Lord. In this our day it is, if you find anything to do, do it. You hear a great deal about the Lord’s guidance;

I would not object to this, but the word is, “Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might”, Ecclesiastes 9: 10. If you find anything to do, do it. You are doing the work because it is to be done.

We use the hymn book in a very restrained and restricted way, restricted because of our ignorance of the hymn book. Anyone can give out a well known hymn at an appropriate time in the assembly meeting, but there are many other hymns that would fit, and if the Holy Spirit had His way and intelligence were in us the hymn book would be better used and heaven would be better repaid from it than it is.

As we sit down to partake of the Lord’s supper we are taking it in the light of the assembly and the Lord views us in that light. If others are not there we miss them, if we are with God. The Lord misses them. The Supper belongs to the assembly and every member of the assembly should partake of it. If not, why not? If something is wrong, judge it; there is grace with the Lord to adjust you, so that you should be qualified to respond to His desire.
